task.goal: Explain the abstract idea of feedback loops to mixed-age museum visitors in several meaningfully different ways.
hard_constraints: A tabletop exhibit has 90 seconds of visitor attention, paper and simple movable pieces only.
Do not imply every feedback loop is harmful or that a single example proves a general rule.
Check understanding on a new example, including a visitor who prefers text over manipulation.
task.available_resources: One curator and two prototype sessions.
task.expected_result: An explanation structure and transfer check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Follow the returning effect
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the defining feature visible: an effect travels through a chain and returns to change what started it. A paper board shows three illustrated cards: plant cover → soil moisture → plant growth → plant cover. Visitors slide a paper marker along the arrows; printed captions provide an equally complete reading route. Explain: “Plants can help soil hold water; water can help plants grow. The result feeds back into its starting point.” This reinforcing loop can support useful growth, although other conditions can limit it.

Use 15 seconds for that definition, 30 for tracing, 15 for a contrasting balancing example—getting cold leads someone to add a blanket, reducing how cold they feel—and 30 for transfer. The contrast establishes that feedback can strengthen change or counteract it; neither label means inherently good or bad.

For transfer, show a new example: microphone sound reaches a speaker, the speaker’s sound reaches the microphone, and the sound grows louder. Visitors point to, move a marker along, or underline the returning path and explain what changes next. Include a nearby one-way sound chain as a distractor.

The outcome depends on recognizing a returning causal influence, rather than merely noticing arrows or repeated events. Prerequisites are readable captions and understandable causal links. The simplified examples omit delays and competing influences; they illustrate structures rather than prove universal behavior. One curator can make the board, cards, and marker from paper.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, compare the tracing board with the same examples presented as ordinary paragraphs. Give both groups the unfamiliar microphone transfer task within the 90-second visit. Record whether visitors identify the return connection and predict its effect, including visitors choosing text only. Revise confusing arrows or captions once; use session two to repeat the comparison. The mechanism is challenged if visitors successfully trace the plant diagram but cannot distinguish the new loop from the one-way chain, or perform no better than paragraph readers. Small prototype samples support design decisions, not a general effectiveness claim.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Let yesterday’s result set tomorrow’s action
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach feedback through successive rounds: what happens now changes what happens next. A paper strip represents a room’s warmth, with a movable temperature marker and a reversible heater card. A printed rule says: “Below the target: heater on. At or above the target: heater off.” In each simplified round, an on heater moves the marker one space warmer; an off heater lets it move one space cooler. Visitors run three rounds, or read a completed three-round strip with identical explanations.

Allocate 10 seconds to the rule, 30 to rounds, 20 to explanation, and 30 to transfer. Explain: “The room’s warmth changes the heater’s action; that action changes the room’s warmth. The result becomes information for the next action.” This balancing feedback keeps warmth near a target in the paper model. A short contrasting strip shows reinforcing feedback: more people share a story, more people see it, and more people can share it. Feedback can therefore regulate or amplify; its value depends on circumstances.

Transfer uses a new scenario: a library adds copies when a waiting list grows, and extra copies shorten that list. Ask visitors to complete or select the next two causal steps and say whether the response counters or strengthens the original change. All answers can be written or spoken without moving pieces.

The mechanism depends on visitors connecting successive rounds, not just obeying the heater rule. It assumes comfort with a short sequence. The temperature model deliberately omits realistic timing and heat loss; it demonstrates feedback rather than predicts an actual room. Materials are two strips, a marker, rule cards, and a heater card.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, compare the round-based activity with a static explanation of the same heater example. Use the library scenario for both, asking why adding copies affects the next decision. Inspect whether visitors connect outcome to subsequent action rather than merely name a desired temperature. Check the completed-strip text route separately. After one revision, repeat in session two. Failure to explain the unfamiliar return connection, despite correctly following the heater rule, would undermine the proposed learning mechanism.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Find the missing return connection
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach feedback by contrasting otherwise similar systems and asking what makes them different. Two paper panels show a person watering a pot. In one, a timer triggers watering without checking the soil. In the other, soil dryness changes the watering decision, watering changes soil moisture, and moisture informs the next decision. A removable paper arrow completes the second panel. Visitors place it, or choose between two printed sentences describing the missing connection.

Use 15 seconds to read the panels, 25 to choose the connection, 20 for explanation, and 30 for transfer. Explain: “A repeating action is not automatically feedback. Feedback happens when an action’s result returns to influence what happens next.” The moisture example shows a potentially useful balancing loop. Add a brief reinforcing example: encouragement can increase practice, improvement can bring more encouragement. Reinforcement can help, while outcomes still depend on other influences; the example establishes no general rule about encouragement.

Transfer presents a new pair: a museum changes queue staffing on a fixed timetable, versus changing staffing after checking queue length, with staffing then affecting the queue. Visitors identify which description contains feedback and underline or state the return connection. Ask what could happen to staffing after the queue shrinks. Both manipulation and text routes contain the full explanation and check.

The working principle is learning the boundary between repetition and feedback through a minimally different pair. It assumes visitors understand that watering and staffing affect the measured conditions. Its limit is that real systems may contain additional, unseen loops; describe only the loop shown. One curator needs illustrated panels, arrow pieces, and sentence cards.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, compare the paired-panel activity with a single closed-loop watering explanation of similar length. Give both versions the same queue transfer check within 90 seconds. Look for correct identification plus an explanation of how the result changes the next action; identifying the more sensible system alone is insufficient. Include text-preferring visitors. Revise once and repeat in session two. If paired-panel visitors still classify fixed repetition as feedback, or cannot explain the new return connection, the contrast has failed its intended purpose. Any advantage remains provisional with two small sessions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict what a small change will do
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make feedback understandable through prediction: does a small change eventually strengthen itself or produce a response that pushes back? A paper board shows a seesaw-shaped diagram with two connected quantities: room warmth and heater activity. Each connection has a plain-language rule: “More warmth means less heating”; “More heating means more warmth.” Visitors place “more” or “less” paper tabs beside the quantities, or read and complete equivalent printed sentences.

Spend 15 seconds introducing the question, 25 predicting the response to extra warmth, 20 explaining and contrasting, and 30 on transfer. Explain: “Extra warmth reduces heating, which pushes warmth back down. When an effect returns to change its starting condition, that is feedback.” Contrast with interest in a collection: more interest can bring more displays, and more displays can attract more interest. One response counters an initial change; the other strengthens it. Neither pattern is inherently helpful or harmful.

The learning mechanism is qualitative prediction, rather than recognizing a circular picture. Transfer presents a new example: more bicycle use encourages more cycle lanes, and more cycle lanes encourage bicycle use. Visitors predict the returning effect of an initial decrease in bicycle use and explain the connection. The text route supplies exactly the same relationships and asks for a written or spoken answer.

One curator can prepare two boards and reusable word tabs. This assumes visitors understand “more” and “less” and accept the stated relationships. Predictions concern these simplified relationships only: delays, thresholds, and competing causes could change real outcomes.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, compare prediction-before-explanation with a same-length version that supplies the worked predictions immediately. Give both the bicycle transfer check within 90 seconds, including visitors choosing text only. Count an answer as successful only if it explains how the initial decrease returns to influence bicycle use. Correct labels alone are insufficient. Revise confusing wording, then repeat in session two. If visitors handle the worked example but reverse the unfamiliar returning effect, or show no useful advantage over the comparator, the proposed prediction mechanism needs reconsideration. Small samples provide provisional design evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Discover a loop that nobody controls
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use two viewpoints to reveal how feedback can emerge when each participant responds locally. Two large paper cards describe a fictional museum display. The visitor card says, “When the display has more interesting contributions, visitors leave more contributions.” The curator card says, “When visitors leave more contributions, the curator has more material to display.” A visitor and companion each read one card and answer, “What changes your action, and what does your action change?” A solo visitor reads both viewpoints. Movable contribution slips are optional; a complete printed dialogue supports visitors who prefer text.

Allocate 15 seconds to the viewpoints, 25 to exchanging or reading the answers, 20 to explanation, and 30 to transfer. Explain: “Each side changes something the other side responds to. Those effects return to influence where they began. That makes a feedback loop, even though nobody controls the whole process.” This fictional loop can support participation, but limited space or unsuitable contributions could interrupt it. Briefly contrast a balancing relationship: a longer queue prompts more staff, and more staff shorten the queue. Feedback can strengthen a change or counter it; usefulness depends on circumstances.

For transfer, present a new text-only scenario: a plant provides shelter for insects; those insects pollinate the plant, helping it produce more plants. Ask visitors to explain the loop from either participant’s viewpoint and predict how fewer insects could eventually affect insect shelter. They may speak, write, or arrange sentence cards.

The mechanism is perspective-taking: connecting individually understandable responses into a system-level relationship. One curator needs viewpoint cards, a printed dialogue, and optional slips. It assumes accessible reading or companion support. Anthropomorphic wording should not imply that plants or insects deliberately manage the loop.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, compare the viewpoint version with a single paragraph containing the same causal facts and definition. Use the unfamiliar plant–insect check for both within 90 seconds. Inspect whether visitors explain both directions and the returning consequence, including a text-preferring visitor using the printed dialogue. Choosing “they help each other” without describing the return is insufficient. Revise once and repeat in session two. If viewpoint readers remember the participants but cannot connect their effects, or infer that feedback requires cooperation or intention, the mechanism has failed its intended purpose. These sessions cannot establish general effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Match the relationships, not the objects
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Teach feedback through explicit analogy: two situations can work alike even when their objects look unrelated. A paper board pairs a bucket-level regulator with a museum suggestion system. In the first simplified model, a low water level opens an inlet; incoming water raises the level; the higher level closes the inlet. In the second, reports of unreadable labels prompt larger lettering; larger lettering reduces reading difficulties; fewer difficulty reports reduce the need for further enlargement. Visitors match three relationship cards across the stories: “current condition,” “response,” and “changed condition affects the response.” A fully printed, aligned text version provides the same mapping without moving pieces.

Allocate 15 seconds to reading, 25 to matching, 20 to explanation, and 30 to transfer. Explain: “The objects differ, but both have a result that comes back to influence the process producing it. That returning influence makes feedback.” Briefly add that feedback can also strengthen change: more sharing can produce more readers, who can produce more sharing. Whether either pattern helps depends on the circumstances.

The proposed mechanism is abstraction through correspondence: explicitly matching causal roles may help visitors recognize feedback beyond the example they learned. This differs from simply showing several examples because visitors must identify what stays structurally the same.

One curator needs one illustrated board, three matching cards, and a text sheet. The approach assumes visitors understand the stated relationships; short captions or companion reading may support younger visitors. The examples are conditional models, not evidence that real systems always behave this way. Reading and comparison may exceed some visitors’ attention, which the prototypes must inspect.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session one, alternate the mapping version with a simple comparator containing the same stories and definition but no matching task or aligned roles. Both must fit 90 seconds. Transfer uses a new fictional case: crowding leads animals to leave a patch, reducing crowding and subsequent departures. Ask visitors to identify the returning influence and explain what happens to departures as crowding falls. Accept spoken or written answers, and include a visitor choosing the complete text route. Correctly matching training cards alone does not count. Revise once, then repeat in session two. Failure to explain the unfamiliar return, or no practical advantage over the simpler comparator, weakens the case for the extra mapping step. Two small sessions provide provisional design evidence only.

EXPAND.title: Stop one link and predict the difference
EXPAND.proposal:
Teach feedback through a counterfactual intervention: discover what a returning influence does by temporarily blocking it. A paper panel describes a simplified school club: more members invite friends; those friends join and can invite others. A paper flap covers the invitation link. Visitors predict what changes when invitations stop, then uncover the explanation. A complete printed version offers the same prediction and reveal without handling pieces.

Allocate 15 seconds to the story, 25 to blocking and predicting, 20 to explanation, and 30 to transfer. Explain: “Feedback happens when a change produces effects that return to influence that same change. Blocking a connection helps us see what the return contributes.” Invitations can reinforce membership growth, but space, interest, and other conditions can limit it. A short contrasting caption explains that checking room temperature and adjusting heating can counter temperature changes. Neither pattern is inherently helpful or harmful.

Transfer uses a new example: a tank’s rising water lifts a float, the float closes an inlet, and reduced inflow slows the rise. Ask what happens if the float no longer controls the inlet, and which returning influence has been interrupted. Visitors may answer aloud, point to a printed answer, or write.

The learning mechanism is comparing an intact causal system with a deliberately interrupted version. It assumes visitors understand invitations and water inflow. The model isolates one loop; stopping invitations does not imply that all membership growth stops. One curator can make two paper panels and a flap. Causal claims must be printed explicitly so visitors need not supply specialist knowledge.
EXPAND.experiment: In session one, alternate the intervention version with an equally brief explanation showing the intact club loop. Give both groups the tank problem within 90 seconds, including text-preferring visitors. Count success only when visitors identify the broken return connection and explain its consequence under the stated assumptions. Merely predicting that the tank fills is insufficient. Revise wording once and repeat in session two. If visitors say every activity stops whenever one connection is blocked, or cannot transfer beyond invitations, the intervention has taught an unreliable shortcut. Small samples provide provisional design evidence.

EXPAND.title: Build one explanation from separate viewpoints
EXPAND.proposal:
Teach feedback by integrating locally understandable facts into a system-level explanation. Three paper cards describe a simplified pond: “More algae makes the water cloudier”; “Cloudier water reduces light for underwater plants”; “Fewer underwater plants leaves more nutrients available for algae.” Visitors arrange the cards beside a shared question: “How could an initial increase in algae help further algae growth?” A printed paragraph provides an equivalent text-only route.

Use 15 seconds to introduce the question, 25 to assemble or read the facts, 20 for explanation, and 30 for transfer. Explain: “Each fact describes one influence. Together they show an effect returning to influence its starting condition: feedback.” The mechanism is explanatory integration: visitors must use several local relationships to explain a consequence that none describes alone. A caption contrasts this reinforcing pattern with balancing feedback, such as sweating reducing the warmth that triggered sweating. Effects and their desirability depend on circumstances.

For transfer, supply three new facts: a longer café queue prompts an extra server; the extra server increases serving capacity; greater capacity shortens the queue, which influences whether the extra server stays. Ask visitors to explain how the café’s response could reduce its original trigger. Accept a spoken or written sentence, or selection of a complete causal explanation from printed choices.

One curator needs two sets of large-print paper cards and matching reading panels. The approach assumes visitors can connect three short statements; younger visitors may share reading with a companion. The pond relationships are stipulated features of a simplified model, not a claim that all ponds behave this way. Limited nutrients, delays, and other influences can change real outcomes.
EXPAND.experiment: In session one, compare the integration question with the same facts already connected in an explanatory paragraph. Both versions include the feedback definition and café transfer check. Inspect whether visitors explain the full return influence rather than recall isolated pond facts. Include visitors choosing text only and note reading difficulties separately from causal errors. Revise once and inspect again in session two. The mechanism is weakened if assembling facts consumes the visit or produces no coherent explanation of the new café loop. No advantage should be claimed from a few successful visitors.

EXPAND.title: Follow a disturbance, rather than a circulating object
EXPAND.proposal:
Explain feedback by asking whether a small disturbance is strengthened or reduced after its consequences return. Two paper accordion strips unfold into short causal explanations. One begins “A little more practice,” followed by “skill improves,” “practice feels more rewarding,” and “motivation for more practice increases.” The other begins “A little warmer,” followed by “more sweating,” “more evaporative cooling,” and “the original warming is reduced.” Visitors place a paper “strengthens” or “counters” label, or read and select the equivalent printed statements.

Allocate 10 seconds to the starting changes, 30 to the two strips, 20 to explanation, and 30 to transfer. Explain: “Feedback is an influence returning to affect the condition that started it. Ask whether the returning effect strengthens that change or pushes against it.” This emphasizes the direction of response, rather than treating feedback as an object traveling around arrows. Neither response is automatically good or bad. The practice example assumes improvement is rewarding; sweating assumes evaporation can provide cooling. These are conditional illustrations, not universal rules.

Transfer presents a new simplified system: an animal population increases; food per animal decreases; fewer young survive; this reduces subsequent population growth. Ask which starting change the consequences affect and whether they strengthen or counter it. Add: “Does that guarantee a steady population?” The supplied explanation says no: timing and other influences matter. Answers may be spoken, written, or selected from text.

One curator can prepare two foldable strips and a transfer card. The prerequisite is understanding comparative words such as more, fewer, and reduced. No arithmetic is required. This approach deliberately omits realistic magnitudes and cannot establish stability from the direction of response alone.
EXPAND.experiment: In session one, compare the disturbance-focused strips with a short definition and the same examples presented without the starting-change questions. Test both on the population example within 90 seconds, explicitly including text-preferring visitors. Look for identification of the returning influence and a justified prediction that it counters the initial increase. Revise once and repeat in session two. If visitors merely associate “fewer” with balancing, or insist that counteracting feedback guarantees stability, the approach has failed its intended distinction. Results remain exploratory.

EXPAND.title: Match the same pattern across different stories
EXPAND.proposal:
Make feedback understandable through explicit analogy: visitors match the causal roles in two very different stories, then express their shared structure without either story’s vocabulary. What changes the outcome is recognizing the same relationship across different subject matter, rather than remembering one example.

Use two parallel paper rows. The first reads: “Bread stock falls → the baker notices the shortage → the baker makes more bread → stock rises, changing the next baking decision.” The second reads: “A person gets warmer → their body responds with sweating → evaporation cools them → their temperature changes the sweating response.” Matching symbols identify condition, response, and effect on the original condition. Visitors pair corresponding cards, or read a complete text alignment with no manipulation required.

Spend 10 seconds introducing the stories, 25 matching their roles, and 20 stating the shared explanation: “Feedback happens when a condition causes effects that return to influence that condition.” A brief caption adds: “These responses counter the starting change. Feedback can also strengthen change: more participation can attract further participation. Either pattern can help or cause problems, depending on circumstances.” Reserve 35 seconds for transfer.

The new example describes a messaging group: more posts prompt more notifications; notifications bring members back; returning members write more posts. Ask visitors to identify the condition, response, and returning effect, then explain whether the original change is strengthened or countered. Offer spoken, written, and fully printed answer-selection routes.

One curator can prepare two matching rows, six movable cards, and a transfer panel. Familiarity with bread stocks and sweating is assumed; causal relationships are supplied explicitly. Younger visitors may need a companion to read. Sweating assumes effective evaporation, and the stories simplify timing and competing influences. Whether matching roles helps visitors abstract the idea remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: Across two prototype sessions, alternate the analogy version with a simple comparator containing the same stories, definition, timing, and transfer question, but no explicit role alignment. In session one, inspect whether visitors understand the role labels and finish within 90 seconds; revise confusing wording. In session two, check whether visitors can explain the returning influence in the unseen messaging example without relying on matching symbols. Include a visitor who chooses the text-only route. The mechanism is challenged if visitors match the teaching cards successfully but cannot identify what the returning effect changes, or show no clearer transfer than the comparator. Treat the small sessions as diagnostic evidence, not proof of superiority.
